title: Trump says his deportation crackdown 'might have been too tough' after midterm losses
excerpt: In a '60 Minutes' interview that aired Sunday, President Donald Trump said his deportation policy 'might have been too tough' — and floated working with Democrats on an immigration deal.
content:
President Donald Trump said his administration's deportation policy "might have been too tough," in his first major interview since Democrats won control of both the House and Senate in the November 3 midterm elections.

In a CBS "60 Minutes" interview with correspondent Ross Douthat that aired Sunday, November 8, Trump said his immigration crackdown "both helped and hurt" him at the polls. "I think it might be too tough, yeah," he said when asked about the deportation policy.

Trump said he believes he earned "an A+ for closing up the border" and "very high marks for getting the bad ones out." But he added that he was hurt because "we also took people that had good jobs, that — that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally."

The president also said he thinks he can work with the incoming Democratic majority in Congress on "some kind of immigration deal," though he offered no detailed proposal. "The deal would be we would work something out," he said.

What the voters said

The Associated Press surveyed more than 100,000 midterm voters and found about six in 10 said the Trump administration's actions on immigration enforcement had "gone too far." A similar share disapproved of how ICE was doing its job, and about six in 10 voters said immigrants to the U.S. today do more to "help the country" than to "hurt" it.

Latino voters shifted sharply: only about one in three Hispanic voters said they supported a Republican in their local U.S. House race, according to the AP voter poll, after about four in 10 had voted for Trump two years earlier. A separate survey by UnidosUS found a record 14.5 million Latinos voted on November 3, with two out of three casting ballots for Democrats in House races.

The other side of the message

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer scoffed at the president's remarks on social media on Sunday, writing: "Trump says his immigration crackdown went too far." Democrats have argued the enforcement campaign itself — not just its tone — is the problem, and it is not yet clear what kind of deal, if any, either side would accept.

At the same time, Trump on Friday named Stephen Miller — the chief architect of his hard-line immigration agenda — as his new White House chief of staff, starting today, Monday, November 9. That appointment sits uneasily beside the president's new language, and it is the first test of whether the shift in words becomes a shift in policy.

What it means for Laredo

Laredo is a border community where immigration enforcement is not an abstract debate — it is daily life, family, work and the local economy. Any change in enforcement posture, or any immigration deal, would be felt here first. Webb Watch 956 will keep reporting what Washington does, not just what it says, and what it means for the 956.
